title: Achieve and Thrive: A Research-Based Guide to Pupil Motivation and Engagement https://www.ambition.org.uk/pupil-engagement-guide/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), January 3, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers Steve Farndon's Achieve and Thrive, a research-based guide (published via the Ambition Institute) synthesizing self-determination theory into practical classroom guidance on pupil motivation and engagement. The guide's central argument is that meeting students' three psychosocial needs — competence, relatedness, and autonomy — is what drives genuine intrinsic motivation, and that external regulation (rules, routines, rewards) functions best as a safety net rather than the primary lever. Farndon explains how motivation can be internalized over time, moving from purely external compliance toward students owning the value of their learning and behaviour. Barton pulls out concrete classroom strategies: build mastery experiences where success is achievable but not guaranteed, get to know students individually to build relatedness, and use invitational language ('you might want to…') rather than commands to nurture a sense of ownership and agency.
points: Overreliance on external regulation (rules, rewards, routines) as the primary motivator can be counterproductive — it can undermine the internal motivation it's meant to eventually replace.
Students need genuine mastery experiences: challenging tasks where success is attainable but not guaranteed, not tasks engineered to avoid all early failure.

Building relatedness is concrete and small-scale — greeting students by name, acknowledging their interests, and encouraging their contributions measurably builds the sense of belonging that fuels motivation.
Supporting autonomy isn't the same as offering unlimited choice — it means helping students understand and internalize the reasons behind expectations and learning goals.
Small language shifts matter: framing a suggestion as “you might want to…” rather than “you need to…” supports a student's sense of ownership and agency.
quotes: This is an important process, because where pupils do feel these three things – or in the language used in self-determination theory, where their needs for relatedness, competence and autonomy are met – their motivation to engage with school increases

However, overreliance on external regulation, especially for motivating learning, can be counterproductive. It can undermine the development of internal motivation and may even reduce intrinsic motivation over time.
Students need to be provided with mastery experiences: opportunities to engage in challenging tasks where success is attainable but not guaranteed.
Teachers should make an effort to get to know their students individually, greet them by name, acknowledge their interests, and encourage their contributions.
Using invitational language that emphasizes student choice and control supports agency. For example, phrasing suggestions as "You might want to…" rather than "You need to…".
